1.pericope_label: So I returned and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living: yea, better is he than both they which hath not yet been

schools.summary: Henry catalogues the oppressions, servants and labourers oppressed by masters who take advantage of their necessity, debtors by cruel creditors and creditors by fraudulent debtors, tenants by hard landlords, orphans by treacherous guardians, and worst of all subjects by arbitrary princes and unjust judges; he adds that such things are done under the sun while above the sun righteousness reigns for ever, and observes that the world is a place of weepers.

Gill lists the oppressed by class, subjects by their prince, the stranger and widow and fatherless by unjust judges, the poor by the rich, servants and labourers by their masters, and reports one rabbi’s paraphrase that the writer saw these by a spirit of prophecy and another’s that he here calls back his earlier word about rejoicing in one’s works; he limits the praise of the dead to a judgment made according to sense, without respect to the future state, takes the dead praised for the righteous dead, notes that the line opposes the maxim that a miserable being is better than none at all, and reports that Jewish interpreters have used it to prove the pre-existence of souls.

Clarke gives the word for oppression its full extent, any injury a man can receive in his person, property or good fame, and concludes that where the power is on the side of the oppressors there is neither protection nor comfort for the oppressed; he counts those happy who have escaped from the pilgrimage of life to the place where the wicked cease from troubling. Wesley says the oppression may be by princes or magistrates or other potent persons and that none afforded pity or succour, and states the terms of the praise of the dead plainly, that setting aside the future life, which the writer does not meddle with in this debate, a wise man would not account the present one worth his while.

Ellicott marks the turn from the instability of happiness to the actual misery of the world, asks what the king was about if the traditional authorship holds and whether he could do nothing but express helpless despair, and notes that the word rendered yet in the second verse belongs to later Hebrew and occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament. Keil and Delitzsch show how the infinitive opening the second verse continues the finite verb before it in an adverbially subordinate way, and remark that one Greek translator, by his choice of a word here and earlier, betrays himself as a Jew.

debates: How far does the praise of the dead go? Wesley and Gill both restrict it, Wesley by setting aside the future life which he says the writer does not meddle with here, and Gill by making the judgment one according to sense that regards the dead purely as dead.
Does the writer withdraw his earlier counsel to rejoice in one’s work? Gill reports a rabbi who thought so and answers that he afterwards repeats it.
Can the traditional author have written this? Ellicott asks what the king was about and whether he could do nothing but express helpless despair, and leaves the question standing.
outliers: Ellicott raises the authorship question as a moral objection rather than a literary one, asking why a king who saw such oppression did nothing but lament it.
Keil and Delitzsch identify one Greek translator as a Jew from his rendering of a single word.
Gill reports that Jewish interpreters have drawn the pre-existence of souls out of the verse about the unborn.
themes: a catalogue of the oppressed
power on the side of the oppressor
the dead praised, the unborn preferred
a judgment made according to sense
a king who only laments

4.pericope_label: Again I considered all travail and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour: the fool foldeth his hands together: better is an handful with quietness: there is one alone, and there is not a second

schools.summary: Henry observes that the envied man got his estate neither easily nor dishonestly but by fair dealing, and is envied the more for the reputation his honesty won him; he draws from this what little conscience most men have, since they grudge a neighbour only for being more industrious, which he calls downright diabolism and illustrates from three pairs of rivals in the old histories, and what little comfort useful men may expect, since those who excel in virtue will always be an eye-sore to those who exceed in vice; and he describes the solitary man as one who would be placed alone in the midst of the earth, thinks one mouth enough in a house, and dares not marry for fear of the expense of a family.

Gill fills in the kinds of work meant, the study of arts and sciences and languages and the writing of books, or excellence in the mechanic arts; he reports one rabbi and other interpreters who make the sixth verse the sluggard’s apology, one of them supplying the word saying at the end of the verse before; and he reports a rabbi who took the missing second of the eighth verse to be a friend or a servant or a wife, preferring the wife, since friendship leads to expenses, a servant would be chargeable and a wife more expensive still.

Clarke says men suffer not only by injustice but through envy also, so that the encouragement to act an upright part is very little; he allows that the handful with quietness may be the slothful man vindicating his idleness or the writer’s own reflection; and he draws the covetous man as one who is the centre of his own existence, as intent on getting money as if he had the largest family, and refusing himself the comforts of life out of his own gains. Wesley says the industrious man meets with envy and obloquy instead of honour, and takes the sixth verse for the sluggard’s apology.

Keil and Delitzsch report the reading that makes the fifth verse an objection and the sixth a reply, note that one interpreter lapses here into a hypothesis of dialogue he rejects elsewhere, and hold instead that the unity of thought is preserved, the rest commended being not the rest of sloth but rest against the activity that robs a man of himself; they describe the folded hands as self-destruction, the man feeding on his own flesh; and they prefer to read the particle of the eighth verse as nevertheless rather than also. Ellicott would render the fourth verse skilful work rather than right work, weighs and rejects a literal reading of eating one’s own flesh since there is no exact parallel to the phrase, makes the conduct recommended a golden mean between ruinous sloth and vexatious toil, and suggests that the solitary man may have been the writer’s own case, the verses following on friendship being of a more cheerful tone than the rest of the book.

debates: Whose words are the handful with quietness? Gill, Wesley and Clarke allow them to the sluggard as an apology for idleness, one interpreter even supplying the word saying to introduce them, while Keil and Delitzsch refuse the dialogue and keep the unity of the thought.

Does the fool eat his own flesh or merely his meat? Ellicott reports the literal proposal, that the sluggard does better who eats in quiet, and rejects it for want of any exact parallel to the phrase.
What kind of rest is commended? Keil and Delitzsch insist it is not the rest of sloth but rest against the hunting after gain and honour that never has enough.
outliers: Ellicott suggests that the solitary man of the seventh verse may have been the writer’s own case, and notes that the verses on friendship which follow are more cheerful than the rest of the book.
Henry calls the grudging of a neighbour’s honest success downright diabolism and finds three examples of it in the old histories.
Gill reports an interpreter who supplies the word saying at the end of the fifth verse, turning the next into a speech.
themes: envy as the wage of honest work
folded hands and wasted flesh
a handful against two fistfuls
whose voice speaks the proverb
a man with no second beside him

9.pericope_label: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour: for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: if two lie together, then they have heat: and a threefold cord is not quickly broken

schools.summary: Henry observes that a man who labours to maintain those he loves has more satisfaction than the miser in his toil, and applies the union to Christians, who assist each other by encouragement or friendly reproof and warm each other’s hearts in converse; where two are closely joined in holy love, he says, Christ comes to them by his Spirit, and there is the third strand of the cord.

Gill takes the occasion of the passage to be the solitariness of the covetous man just described, and holds it best to take a wife or at least to have a friend, since man is a sociable creature and it was the judgment of God that he should not be alone; he keeps the fall to plain accidents, a man thrown from his horse or into a ditch and lifted up by his companion; and he turns the last verse to spiritual use, since the enemy chooses a believer when alone, as he tempted the first woman in the garden and the Lord in the wilderness, while fellow Christians can help by advice and by striving together in prayer.

Clarke holds bluntly that married life is infinitely to be preferred to the solitary life, for the very reasons alleged below, which he says require no explanation. Wesley keeps the passage general, two who live together in any kind of society and so support and encourage and strengthen each other.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that the marriage relation is not excluded but remains in the background, the author having two friends in his eye who lie under one covering on a cold night, a proof of friendship treated as such in a rabbinic tract also; they report that one version has confused the word for woe with another, observe that the verb about raising the fallen man is potential rather than certain and holds good provided the companion is a true friend, and object that the conditional particles will not allow the merely logical reading of the last verse, seeing no reason why its verb should not carry a sudden assault as well as a completed subjugation. Ellicott notes that the word for woe occurs only once besides in the book though common in later Hebrew, and that nights in that country were often very cold, sleeping with no covering but the ordinary day garment seeming to have been common.

debates: Is the passage about marriage or friendship? Gill and Clarke read it of marriage, Clarke calling married life infinitely preferable, while Keil and Delitzsch keep the marriage relation in the background and find two friends in view; Henry applies it to Christian fellowship.

What does the verb of the twelfth verse mean? One interpreter takes it as overpowering, so that one can overpower a solitary man while two hold their ground; Keil and Delitzsch object that the conditional particles forbid so logical a reading and allow the sense of a sudden assault.
Is the lifting up of the fallen man certain? Keil and Delitzsch call the verb potential rather than certain, holding good provided the companion is a true friend.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch cite a rabbinic tract in which two sleeping under one covering is taken as evidence of friendship.
Ellicott explains the warmth of the eleventh verse from the cold nights of the country and the practice of sleeping under nothing but the day garment.
Henry makes the third strand of the cord the presence of Christ with two who are joined in holy love.
themes: a wife, a friend, or a fellow Christian
the companion who lifts the fallen
warmth under one covering
a verb between assault and conquest
the third strand of the cord

13.pericope_label: Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished: for out of prison he cometh to reign: I considered all the living which walk under the sun with the second child that shall stand up in his stead

schools.summary: Henry allows the writer to speak freely on kingship because he was himself a king, and holds that nothing is more slippery than the highest post of honour without wisdom and the people’s love, and that it is so far from being any part of the honour of kings not to be admonished that it is their greatest dishonour, since folly and wilfulness commonly go together and those who most need admonition can worst bear it.

Gill draws the two portraits, the old king otherwise venerable for gravity and dignity but of small capacity and vicious with it, and the youth not yet come to manhood, poor and disadvantaged by a poor education, his parents unable to buy him books or masters; he instances the young man sold into Egypt, whom a rabbinic source names here, and the youngest son taken from the sheepfold to the throne, while reporting one scholar who reads the line of the old king coming out of a degenerate house, the figure being of a degenerate vine; and he calls the fickleness of the last verses an itch of novelty passing from generation to generation.

Clarke reports an old paraphrase that finds the whole passage in the patriarch, a poor child of three years who refused the idols the old foolish king had set up, was cast into a furnace and delivered by a miracle, and afterwards left the country of the idolaters to reign over another land while his persecutor grew poor; dissatisfied with the ancient guesses, he offers a reconstruction of his own in which a jealous king imprisons a promising son who is later brought out and set on the throne, only to be corrupted by power and flattery in his turn; and he quotes two Latin lines on fortune making a consul out of a rhetorician and a Roman writer on most people adoring the rising sun. Wesley counts three generations in the last verse, the authors of the change, their parents and their children, all of the same inclination, so that they will weary of a wise successor as their parents wearied of his foolish predecessor.

Ellicott says at the outset that the section presents great difficulties, that the context gives little help because of the abruptness with which a new subject is introduced, and that no confidence can be placed in attempts to find a definite historical reference; he finds the Hebrew ambiguous over whether the poverty belongs to the old king or the new; and on the second youth he parts company with most modern interpreters, who identify him with the young man of the earlier verse, answering that by no stretch of rhetoric can all the living who walk under the sun be taken for the subjects of one sovereign, and preferring to read a generation displaced by a new one with which the generation after will be just as dissatisfied. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase about the king who will no longer be warned as a tolerative passive, a refusal to let oneself be enlightened, and describe him as hardened in his old age and undermining his own throne; they keep the succession of kings and note that the words place the author back at the time of the change of government.

debates: Who is the second youth of the fifteenth verse? Most modern interpreters, as Ellicott reports, identify him with the young man of the thirteenth; Ellicott answers that all the living who walk under the sun cannot be the subjects of one sovereign, and reads instead of a generation displaced by the next.

Is there a historical reference behind the passage? Clarke reports an ancient paraphrase finding it in the patriarch and Nimrod, Gill instances the young man sold into Egypt and the youngest son taken from the sheepfold, while Ellicott says no confidence can be placed in any such attempt.

Whose poverty is spoken of in the fourteenth verse? Ellicott finds the Hebrew as ambiguous as the English over whether the old king or the new is meant; Gill reports one scholar who refers the whole line to the old king coming out of a degenerate house.
outliers: Clarke, dissatisfied with the ancient guesses, constructs a story of his own: a jealous king imprisons a promising son, who is freed and enthroned to popular joy and then corrupted by power and flattery.
Henry notes that the writer may speak freely of the vanity of kingly dignity because he was himself a king.
Clarke quotes two Latin lines on fortune making a consul out of a rhetorician, and adds a Roman writer’s remark that most people adore the rising sun.
themes: a king too old to be warned
the prison and the throne
a paraphrase that names the patriarch
one sovereign or one generation
the rising sun and the setting one
